Nṛti in one passage of the Atharvaveda seems to mean a bag of skin. But though the Paippalāda recension has the same text, it is clear that we must read dṛti with Roth and Whitney. Ludwig renders the word ‘dancer,’ which makes no sense in the context.
Foot notes vi. 18, 3.
St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v.
Translation of the Atharvaveda, 294. Cf. Weber, Indische Studien, 5, 235; Bloomfield, Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 468.
Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 514.

Nṛtū occurs once in the Rigveda denoting a female ‘dancer.’ In another passage nṛti is found coupled with hāsa, ‘laughter,’ in the description of the funeral ritual; but though it is clear that a joyful celebration is meant (like the Irish ‘wake’ or the old-fashioned feasting in Scotland after a funeral), it is difficult to be certain that actual dancing is here meant. Dancing is, however, often referred to in the Rigveda and later. Nṛttagīta, ‘dance and song,’ are mentioned in the Jaiminīya brāhmaṇa as found in the sixth world. See also śailūṣa.
Foot notes i. 92, 4 (where Uṣas, Goddess of Dawn, is compared to a dancer).
